what_happened: The operator closed pull request #129 by hand and left a comment saying it was superseded by #130. Job 60r4's content had already landed inside #130, because job sg0j was built on top of 60r4's unmerged work. Athena does not close a pull request whose work reached main through a later one, so #129 would have stayed open and redundant.
cause: Athena lets a job be built on an earlier unmerged job's branch, but it doesn't record that dependency or track the earlier pull request. When the later pull request merges, nothing links it to the earlier ones whose commits it carries. The lifecycle treats each pull request as independent, so the earlier job stays open until a person notices. The operator already knows this gap as 6ejp.
prevention: Record the base job or pull request whenever a job is cut on top of an unmerged job. After any pull request merges, check each recorded earlier pull request that is still open. If all of its commits are now reachable from main, close it automatically. The comment should name the superseding pull request and job, and the earlier job should be marked as landed via the later one. If the commits are not all reachable, flag the pull request to the operator instead of closing it.
proposed_request: When a pull request merges and carries commits from earlier unmerged jobs (stacked jobs), Athena should detect those earlier jobs' open pull requests and close each one that is fully contained in main. The comment should name the superseding pull request and job, and the earlier job's state should show it landed via the later one. If an earlier pull request is only partly contained, leave it open and flag it to the operator. Show this works with the case of PR #129 (job 60r4), whose content landed in PR #130 (job sg0j): the system closes #129 with no manual step. Cover the contained and partly-contained cases with tests.
